quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on bits, nibbles, bases and the conventions of hexadecimal weave notation.

questions.q: Why can a pick of a weave be treated as a binary number?
options: Because picks are inserted two at a time
Because each end is either lifted (1) or not (0)
Because the loom has two shafts
Because the reed has two wires per dent
questions.explain: Across one pick every end is in one of two states, up or down, so the row of ends is a string of ones and zeros — a binary number.

questions.q: What is a nibble?
questions.explain: A nibble is four bits, exactly the amount one hexadecimal digit represents. Eight bits is a byte.

questions.q: How many different values can one hexadecimal digit represent?
questions.explain: Hex digits run 0–9 then A–F, sixteen symbols in all, matching the sixteen possible four-bit patterns.

questions.q: In hexadecimal, the digit A stands for which decimal value?
questions.explain: A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15. Sixteen itself is written $10.

questions.q: In the lecture's weave notation the picks are written from the bottom of the point paper upward, one hex number per pick.
questions.explain: The convention is first code = first pick at the bottom, with the most significant bit on the left end.

questions.q: What does the suffix −3 mean in $8 $4 $2 −3?
options: The design is three ends wide
questions.explain: The appended −n gives the width in ends; it tells the decoder how many of the bits are real ends and how many are idle padding.

questions.q: When a weave's width is not a multiple of four, where are the idle zero ends added before grouping into hex digits?
options: On the left of each pick
On the right of each pick
questions.explain: For weaves the padding goes on the right of each pick, so the real ends keep their positions from the left. A plain number is padded on the left because leading zeros do not change its value.

questions.q: Why is a hex list useful on the mill floor?
options: It can be read directly by a CAD system or an electronic dobby
It tells the weaver the picks per inch
questions.explain: The lecture notes that a short list of hex numbers, one per pick, can be fed straight into CAD software or an electronic dobby.

questions.q: The symbol $ in front of a code, as in $6D, marks the number as hexadecimal.
questions.explain: The lecture writes hex values with a leading $, e.g. 109 = $6D; the converter accepts the number with or without it.

questions.q: The code $9 $C $6 $3 −4 in the lecture decodes to which weave?
questions.explain: 1001, 1100, 0110, 0011 — each pick lifts two adjacent ends and the pair moves one end along per pick: the 2/2 twill.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Place values, bit grouping and what changes when the width or the base changes.

questions.q: The decimal value of a binary number is found by
options: Summing each 1 multiplied by its power of two, counted from the right starting at 2⁰
questions.explain: Each bit position is a power of two; 1101 = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13. Simply adding the digits would give 3.

questions.q: How many bits are needed to write one pick of a 12-end weave, and how many hex digits does that make?
questions.explain: Twelve ends are twelve bits; grouped in fours they form 12 ÷ 4 = 3 hex digits with no padding needed.

questions.q: A weave is 6 ends wide. How many hex digits are written per pick and how many idle ends are added?
questions.explain: Six bits must be rounded up to eight, i.e. two hex digits, which means two zero ends are added on the right.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of $10?
questions.explain: In hexadecimal the second column is sixteens, so $10 = 1 × 16 + 0 = 16.

questions.q: Adding zeros on the left of a binary number changes its value.
questions.explain: Leading zeros do not change a number's value, which is why the converter pads on the left. Weave padding is different: it goes on the right and is dropped when decoding.

questions.q: If a 4-end pick is coded $F, what does the pick do?
questions.explain: $F = 1111, so every end in the group is up and the pick floats under all four.

questions.q: Moving from a 4-end to a 16-end weave, how do the hex digits per pick change?
questions.explain: Hex digits per pick = ends ÷ 4, so 4 ends need 1 digit and 16 ends need 4.

questions.q: In the code $8 $4 $2 −3, which end is lifted on the first (bottom) pick?
questions.explain: $8 = 1000; after dropping the idle fourth bit the pick is 100, so only end 1 is up. $4 lifts end 2 and $2 lifts end 3 — a 1/2 twill.

questions.q: How many different lift patterns are possible on one pick of a 4-end weave?
questions.explain: Four bits give 2⁴ = 16 patterns, from 0000 to 1111 — one for each hex digit.

questions.q: The most significant bit of each pick's code corresponds to the left-hand end of the design.
questions.explain: The lecture's convention places the most significant bit on the left end, so the first end of the design is the leftmost bit.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Conversions between binary, decimal and hex, including the lecture's own examples, and coding small weaves.

questions.q: Convert the binary number 1101101 to decimal.
What is the decimal value of $6D?
Convert $24A9E to decimal.
The binary number 1010001001100 equals $144C. What is its decimal value?
What is the decimal value of the binary nibble 1011?
questions.explain: 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11, written $B in hex.

questions.q: Convert $FF to decimal.
questions.explain: $FF = 15 × 16 + 15 = 255, the largest value of two hex digits (eight ends all up).

questions.q: A pick of an 8-end weave lifts ends 1, 2, 7 and 8 and sinks the rest. Write its hex code and give the decimal value of that code.
questions.explain: The row is 1100 0011 = $C3; decimal 12 × 16 + 3 = 195.

questions.q: A 2/1 twill on 3 ends has picks 110, 011, 101 (bottom first). Padding on the right, what is its hex code?
questions.explain: Padded rows are 1100, 0110, 1010 = $C, $6, $A. Padding on the left would give $6 $3 $5, which is the plain-number convention, not the weave convention.

questions.q: Plain weave on 4 ends has picks 1010 and 0101. Its hex code is
questions.explain: 1010 = $A and 0101 = $5, so $A $5 −4 (reading from the bottom pick). $9 $6 would be 1001 and 0110, a different weave.

questions.q: The 2/2 twill is extended to 8 ends: picks 10011001, 11001100, 01100110, 00110011. Its hex code is
questions.explain: Each pick splits into two identical nibbles: 1001 1001 = $99, 1100 1100 = $CC, 0110 0110 = $66, 0011 0011 = $33.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using hex codes with CAD and electronic dobbies, and the mistakes that corrupt a design on the way.

questions.q: A designer sends $8 $4 $2 to the loom but forgets the −3. What is the risk?
options: The system will treat the idle fourth end as real, weaving a 4-end design with a dead end
The picks will be read in reverse order
questions.explain: Without the width the decoder cannot know the fourth bit is padding, so it would weave 4 ends with the last end never lifting.

questions.q: A 10-end mock leno is to be coded. How many hex digits per pick are needed and how many idle ends are added?
questions.explain: Ten bits round up to twelve, i.e. three hex digits, with two zero ends appended on the right of each pick.

questions.q: A student types the weave's first code as the top pick of the point paper. What happens when the lecture's engine draws it?
options: Nothing, the order does not matter
The design appears upside down compared with the intention
questions.explain: The convention is first code = first pick at the bottom; entering picks top-first flips the design vertically.

questions.q: A weave repeats on 20 ends. Why is it convenient for the hex notation?
options: 20 is a multiple of 4, so no idle ends are needed
It needs only one hex digit
questions.explain: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 hex digits exactly, so there is no padding — though the width −20 should still be written so the decoder knows the real width.

questions.q: The converter would read the hex input 6D and $6D as the same number.
questions.explain: The lecture says to type hex with or without the leading $; both give 109.

questions.q: A dobby controller shows the pick code $0 for a pick. What will the loom do on that pick?
questions.explain: $0 = 0000: no end is lifted, so the pick lies on top of all the ends — a float across the whole group.

questions.q: The engine on the Try your own panel also outputs a draft. Why does a designer check it after typing hex codes?
options: To see how many healds the idea needs
To find the picks per inch
questions.explain: The lecture says the draft and peg plan are generated so you can see how many healds your design needs — the practical limit on any dobby loom.

questions.q: A code list reads $9 $C $6 $3 −4 but the sample woven looks like a plain weave. Which single error could explain it?
options: The codes were entered as $A $5 by mistake
questions.explain: $A $5 is 1010, 0101 — plain weave. Omitting the width or reversing pick order would still give a 2/2 twill (possibly flipped), not plain weave.

questions.q: Which is the correct way to pad the 3-end pick 101 for the weave code?
questions.explain: Weave padding goes on the right so the real ends keep their places from the left: 101 → 1010 = $A. Padding on the left would move the ends.

questions.q: A designer wants to code a 4-end 3/1 twill whose picks (bottom first) are 1110, 0111, 1011, 1101. The hex list is
questions.explain: 1110 = $E, 0111 = $7, 1011 = $B, 1101 = $D. The other options either reverse the digit order or swap picks.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step conversions and the subtle difference between padding a number and padding a weave.

questions.q: A pick code for an 8-end weave reads $64. What is its decimal value?
questions.explain: $64 = 6 × 16 + 4 = 100. Note that hex 64 is not decimal 64 — a common slip.

questions.q: What is the decimal value of the binary number 11001100?
questions.explain: 11001100 = 128 + 64 + 8 + 4 = 204, which is $CC — one pick of the 8-end 2/2 twill.

questions.q: The binary 1010001001100 has 13 bits. In the converter it becomes $144C, but if it were a 13-end weave pick, its hex code would be
questions.explain: A weave pick is padded on the right: 1010 0010 0110 0000 = $A260. The converter pads on the left, giving $144C — same bits, different grouping. $A26 drops the padding digit and would change the width to 12.

questions.q: A student converts $C to binary as 1100 and then says the pick lifts ends 3 and 4. What is wrong?
options: The most significant bit is the left end, so 1100 lifts ends 1 and 2
questions.explain: With the most significant bit on the left end, 1100 means ends 1 and 2 up and 3 and 4 down; the student read the bits from the right.

questions.q: The code $8 $4 $1 $2 −4 lifts each end exactly once in four picks.
questions.explain: 1000, 0100, 0001, 0010 — ends 1, 2, 4 and 3 are lifted in turn, one per pick; that is why the lecture calls it a 4-end satinette.

questions.q: How many ends are lifted in total over the four picks of $9 $C $6 $3 −4?
questions.explain: Each of 1001, 1100, 0110 and 0011 contains two 1s, so 4 × 2 = 8 end-lifts in the repeat — half of the 16 squares.

questions.q: Which of these decimal numbers needs exactly two hex digits?
questions.explain: Two hex digits cover 16 ($10) to 255 ($FF). 15 is $F (one digit), 256 is $100 and 4,096 is $1000.

questions.q: A 16-end weave repeat has 16 picks. How many hex digits are needed to write the whole repeat?
questions.explain: 16 ends ÷ 4 = 4 digits per pick, × 16 picks = 64 hex digits in total.

questions.q: Why does the lecture pad weaves on the right but numbers on the left?
options: Because looms read right to left
Because a number's value is unchanged by leading zeros, whereas in a weave each bit is a fixed end position counted from the left
Because hex digits are read backwards
There is no reason; it is a convention only
questions.explain: Zeros on the left of a number are harmless, but inserting zeros on the left of a pick would shift every real end one place along the design.

questions.q: Decoding $A $5 $A $5 −4 gives a plain weave. Decoding $A $5 $A $5 −3 gives
options: The same plain weave on 3 ends
A 3-end weave with picks 101, 010 — a plain-weave with an odd repeat
An error, because 3 ends cannot be plain weave
questions.explain: Dropping the fourth bit leaves 101 and 010: a plain interlacing on an odd width, which would not repeat cleanly as true plain weave across a warp of many ends.
